beats.say: Fifteen pendulums. No motors, no tricks. Just watch what happens at second sixty.

head: SAME START.
DIFFERENT LENGTHS.
beats.say: They all start together. But each string is a little shorter than the one before. Thirty four centimeters, down to twenty one.

head: SHORTER MEANS
FASTER.
beats.say: A shorter pendulum swings faster. In one minute, the longest swings fifty one times. The next, fifty two. The shortest, sixty five.

head: SO THEY
DRIFT APART.
beats.say: So they slowly drift out of step. First a snake. Then what looks like pure chaos. But it isn't.

head: SECOND 30:
2 ROWS.
beats.say: At second thirty, they snap into two rows, swapping sides. Every other pendulum together.

head: SECOND 60:
ALL 15.
beats.say: And at second sixty, every pendulum has finished a whole number of swings. So all fifteen line up again. Perfectly.
Follow Ship With Pip for more.

title: 15 pendulums, no motors. Watch what happens at second 60
caption: 15 pendulums, each a little shorter than the last. A shorter pendulum swings faster (T = 2π√(L/g)), so in 60 seconds the longest swings 51 times, the next 52, and the shortest 65. They drift into snakes and chaos, snap into 2 rows at second 30, and at second 60 every one has done a whole number of swings, so all 15 line up again. Lengths from 34 cm down to 21 cm. Same setup as the Harvard pendulum waves demo, simulated here.
notes: Harvard demo: 15 pendulums, 60 s cycle, longest does 51 oscillations. Pendulum k swings 51+k times per 60 s. L = g*(T/(2*pi))^2 with g = 9.81: longest T = 60/51 = 1.18 s, L = 0.34 m; shortest T = 60/65 = 0.92 s, L = 0.21 m. At 30 s pendulum k has done 25.5 + k/2 (2 rows); at 60 s 51 + k (all whole, aligned). Video time is mapped to sim time (shown as t = ... s on screen), slightly faster than real time.
